exam.title: Mathematics I - Advanced Exam
exam.subtitle: Advanced Abstract and Linear Algebra
exam.instructions: Complete all tasks. Show complete solution approach for all calculations. Proofs must be complete and rigorous. Permitted aids: calculator without programming function. Good luck!

exercises.title: The symmetric group S₃
exercises.description:
a) Determine $(1\,2)\circ(2\,3)$ and $(2\,3)\circ(1\,2)$ in $S_3$ (apply the right permutation first).
b) Determine the orders of all elements and all subgroups.
c) Show that $A_3 = \ker(\operatorname{sgn})$ is a normal subgroup and determine $S_3/A_3$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Products
$(1\,2)\circ(2\,3)$: $1 \to 1 \to 2$, $2 \to 3 \to 3$, $3 \to 2 \to 1$, so $(1\,2\,3)$. $(2\,3)\circ(1\,2)$: $1 \to 2 \to 3$, $3 \to 3 \to 2$, $2 \to 1 \to 1$, so $(1\,3\,2)$. Both different: $S_3$ is not abelian.

Step 2: Part b): Orders and subgroups
Orders: $\mathrm{id}$: $1$; the three transpositions: $2$; the two $3$-cycles: $3$. Subgroups (orders divide $6$): $\{\mathrm{id}\}$, $\{\mathrm{id},(1\,2)\}$, $\{\mathrm{id},(1\,3)\}$, $\{\mathrm{id},(2\,3)\}$, $A_3 = \{\mathrm{id},(1\,2\,3),(1\,3\,2)\}$, $S_3$. No element of order $6$: $S_3$ is not cyclic.

Step 3: Part c): Normal subgroup
The kernel of a homomorphism is always a normal subgroup. $\operatorname{sgn}: S_3 \to \{\pm1\}$ is a homomorphism with kernel $A_3$ (even permutations). Alternatively: $[S_3:A_3] = 2$ and subgroups of index $2$ are normal.

Step 4: Part c): Quotient group
$\operatorname{sgn}$ is surjective. First isomorphism theorem: $S_3/A_3 \cong \{\pm1\} \cong \mathbb{Z}_2$. Size check: $|S_3| = |A_3|\cdot|S_3/A_3| = 3\cdot2 = 6$ ✓. In contrast $\{\mathrm{id},(1\,2)\}$ is **not** normal: $(1\,3)(1\,2)(1\,3)^{-1} = (3\,2) \notin \{\mathrm{id},(1\,2)\}$.

exercises.title: The ring ℤ₁₂
exercises.description:
a) Determine the units and the zero divisors of $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$.
b) Determine all ideals of $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$.
c) Show $\mathbb{Z}_{12} \cong \mathbb{Z}_3\times\mathbb{Z}_4$ by giving an isomorphism.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Units and zero divisors
$a$ is a unit $\iff \gcd(a,12) = 1$: $\{1,5,7,11\}$. Zero divisors are all $a \neq 0$ with $\gcd(a,12) > 1$: $\{2,3,4,6,8,9,10\}$. Example: $3\cdot4 = 12 \equiv 0$.

Step 2: Part b): Ideals
Every subgroup of $(\mathbb{Z}_{12},+)$ is an ideal (cyclic group, subgroups $\langle d\rangle$ for $d \mid 12$). Ideals: $(1) = \mathbb{Z}_{12}$, $(2)$, $(3)$, $(4)$, $(6)$, $(12) = \{0\}$ — so $6$ ideals, corresponding to the divisors of $12$.

Step 3: Part c): Map
$\varphi: \mathbb{Z}_{12} \to \mathbb{Z}_3\times\mathbb{Z}_4$, $\varphi(x) = (x \bmod 3,\ x \bmod 4)$. Well-defined because $3 \mid 12$ and $4 \mid 12$. Homomorphism: residues are compatible with $+$ and $\cdot$; $\varphi(1) = (1,1)$.

Step 4: Part c): Bijectivity
Kernel: $\varphi(x) = (0,0) \iff 3 \mid x$ and $4 \mid x \iff 12 \mid x \iff x = 0$. Injective, and since $|\mathbb{Z}_{12}| = 12 = |\mathbb{Z}_3\times\mathbb{Z}_4|$ also bijective. This is the Chinese remainder theorem ($\gcd(3,4) = 1$). Check: units $\leftrightarrow$ $\mathbb{Z}_3^\times\times\mathbb{Z}_4^\times$ has $2\cdot2 = 4$ elements ✓.

exercises.title: Minimal polynomial of √2 + √3
exercises.description:
Let $\alpha = \sqrt2 + \sqrt3$.
a) Determine a monic polynomial $f \in \mathbb{Q}[x]$ of degree $4$ with $f(\alpha) = 0$.
b) Show that $f$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ and give $[\mathbb{Q}(\alpha):\mathbb{Q}]$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Eliminate the roots
$\alpha - \sqrt2 = \sqrt3 \Rightarrow \alpha^2 - 2\sqrt2\alpha + 2 = 3 \Rightarrow \alpha^2 - 1 = 2\sqrt2\alpha$. Squaring: $(\alpha^2 - 1)^2 = 8\alpha^2 \Rightarrow \alpha^4 - 10\alpha^2 + 1 = 0$. So $f(x) = x^4 - 10x^2 + 1$.

Step 2: Part b): No rational roots
Possible rational roots are $\pm1$: $f(\pm1) = 1 - 10 + 1 = -8 \neq 0$. So no linear factor over $\mathbb{Q}$.

Step 3: Part b): No quadratic factorisation
Ansatz $f = (x^2 + ax + b)(x^2 - ax + c)$ (the coefficient of $x^3$ is $0$). Comparing coefficients: $b + c - a^2 = -10$, $a(c - b) = 0$, $bc = 1$. Case $a = 0$: $b + c = -10$, $bc = 1$, discriminant $100 - 4 = 96$ not a square. Case $c = b$: $b^2 = 1$, so $a^2 = 2b + 10 \in \{12, 8\}$, no rational squares. So irreducible.

Step 4: Part b): Degree
$f$ is the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$, hence $[\mathbb{Q}(\alpha):\mathbb{Q}] = 4$. Since $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha) \subseteq \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)$ and $[\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2,\sqrt3):\mathbb{Q}] = 4$ we get $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha) = \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)$. The four roots of $f$ are $\pm\sqrt2 \pm \sqrt3$.

exercises.title: Jordan form of a 2×2 matrix
exercises.description:
Let $A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$.
a) Determine eigenvalues and eigenspaces. Is $A$ diagonalisable?
b) Determine a Jordan basis and the Jordan normal form.
c) Compute $A^n$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Eigenvalue
$\operatorname{tr}A = 4$, $\det A = 3 + 1 = 4$: $\lambda^2 - 4\lambda + 4 = (\lambda - 2)^2$. Eigenvalue $\lambda = 2$ with algebraic multiplicity $2$.

Step 2: Part a): Eigenspace
$N := A - 2I = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$ has rank $1$, so $\dim\ker N = 1 < 2$. Eigenspace $\operatorname{span}\{(1,-1)\}$. **Not diagonalisable.**

Step 3: Part b): Jordan chain
Choose $\vec v_2$ with $N\vec v_2 \neq \vec0$, e.g. $\vec v_2 = (1,0)$. Then $\vec v_1 := N\vec v_2 = (1,-1)$ (an eigenvector). With $P = (\vec v_1\,|\,\vec v_2) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ we have $P^{-1}AP = J = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$.

Step 4: Part c): Matrix power
$A = 2I + N$ with $N^2 = 0$ (since $N^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$). Binomial theorem: $A^n = 2^nI + n\,2^{n-1}N$, so $A^n = \begin{pmatrix} 2^n + n2^{n-1} & n2^{n-1} \\ -n2^{n-1} & 2^n - n2^{n-1} \end{pmatrix}$.

Step 5: Check
$n = 2$: $\begin{pmatrix} 4+4 & 4 \\ -4 & 4-4 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 8 & 4 \\ -4 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$. Directly: $A^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 9-1 & 3+1 \\ -3-1 & -1+1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 8 & 4 \\ -4 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ ✓.

exercises.title: Euclid, Bézout and remainder theorem
exercises.description:
a) Determine $\gcd(240,46)$ and $x,y$ with $240x + 46y = \gcd(240,46)$.
b) Determine the inverse of $17$ modulo $43$.
c) Solve $x \equiv 2 \pmod 5$, $x \equiv 3 \pmod 7$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Euclidean algorithm
$240 = 5\cdot46 + 10$, $46 = 4\cdot10 + 6$, $10 = 1\cdot6 + 4$, $6 = 1\cdot4 + 2$, $4 = 2\cdot2$. $\gcd = 2$.

Step 2: Part a): Substitute backwards
$2 = 6 - 4 = 2\cdot6 - 10 = 2\cdot46 - 9\cdot10 = 2\cdot46 - 9(240 - 5\cdot46) = 47\cdot46 - 9\cdot240$. So $x = -9$, $y = 47$. Check: $-2160 + 2162 = 2$ ✓.

Step 3: Part b): Inverse
$43 = 2\cdot17 + 9$, $17 = 1\cdot9 + 8$, $9 = 1\cdot8 + 1$. Backwards: $1 = 9 - 8 = 2\cdot9 - 17 = 2\cdot43 - 5\cdot17$. So $17^{-1} \equiv -5 \equiv 38$. Check: $17\cdot38 = 646 = 15\cdot43 + 1$ ✓.

Step 4: Part c): Chinese remainder theorem
$x = 2 + 5k$; $2 + 5k \equiv 3 \pmod 7 \iff 5k \equiv 1 \iff k \equiv 3$ (since $5\cdot3 = 15 \equiv 1$). $x = 2 + 15 = 17$, so $x \equiv 17 \pmod{35}$. Check: $17 \bmod 5 = 2$ ✓, $17 \bmod 7 = 3$ ✓.
